lessons.title: The Old Tax Regime: Higher Rates in Exchange for Deductions

children.text: The old regime is the system your parents filed under. It charges more on every rupee above ₹5 lakh, then hands part of it back if you pay rent, repay a home loan, invest in PPF or ELSS, or buy health insurance. It has not been abolished. It has been moved behind a door marked 'opt out', and you have to walk through that door on purpose.

body.text: Since FY 2023-24 the new regime applies unless you choose otherwise. Salaried employees choose the old regime by declaring it to their employer and confirming it in their income tax return. Nothing happens automatically.

children.text: Old Regime Slabs: Four Bands and an Age Twist

body.caption: Old Tax Regime Slabs, Tax Year 2026-27 (Resident Individuals)

children.text: Two things stand out. First, the jump from 5% straight to 20% at ₹5 lakh is brutal, and 30% arrives at just ₹10 lakh, against ₹24 lakh in the new regime. Second, the old regime gives senior citizens a higher tax-free limit. The new regime uses one slab table for every age, which is one reason some retirees stay with the old regime.

body.title: Tax on the Same Taxable Income: Old vs New (After Rebate, Before Cess, ₹ Thousand)

children.text: Read this chart carefully, because it frames the entire decision. On the same taxable income, the old regime always costs more. At ₹15 lakh the gap is ₹1,57,500. The only way the old regime can win is if your deductions shrink your taxable income far enough to close that gap. The old regime is not a cheaper rate card. It is a more expensive rate card with coupons.

body.title: Old Regime Slab Practice
body.prompt: Farhan, 34, a sales manager in Kolkata, has taxable income of ₹12,00,000 under the old regime after all his deductions. What is his total tax including 4% cess?
body.explanation: Tax up to ₹10 lakh is ₹1,12,500. The next ₹2,00,000 is taxed at 30%, adding ₹60,000. Slab tax is ₹1,72,500. Cess at 4% is ₹6,900. Total: ₹1,79,400.

children.text: The Small Rebate and the ₹5 Lakh Cliff

The old regime has a rebate too, under Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 87A of the 1961 Act). It is worth up to ₹12,500 and applies only when taxable income is ₹5 lakh or less. The standard deduction is ₹50,000, not ₹75,000. And there is no marginal relief: cross ₹5 lakh by a single rupee and the entire ₹12,500 comes back.

stats.label: Result of earning ₹10,000 more
stats.context: No marginal relief in the old regime

body.text: If you are in the old regime and your taxable income lands just above ₹5 lakh, a small extra deduction can be worth more than its own value. A ₹10,000 top-up to your PPF that brings taxable income from ₹5,10,000 down to ₹5,00,000 saves ₹15,080 of tax. Always check where you land relative to ₹5 lakh.

body.title: Spot the True Statement
body.question: Which of these statements about the old regime in tax year 2026-27 is correct?
options: The old regime has marginal relief just above its ₹5 lakh rebate limit
Senior citizens get a higher tax-free limit in the old regime than younger taxpayers
Salaried employees get a ₹75,000 standard deduction in both regimes
Taxpayers are placed in the old regime automatically if they have a home loan
body.explanation: Residents aged 60 to 79 pay nil up to ₹3 lakh and those aged 80 and above pay nil up to ₹5 lakh in the old regime. There is no marginal relief in the old regime, its standard deduction is ₹50,000, and the new regime is the default for everyone regardless of loans.

children.text: The Coupons: What the Old Regime Lets You Claim

markDefs.definition: Your total income from all sources after exemptions, but before deductions like 80C and 80D are subtracted.

children.text: The old regime's benefits come in two layers. Exemptions like HRA and LTA are carved out of your salary first. Deductions like 80C and 80D are then subtracted from your
. Both reduce taxable income, and almost all of them disappear in the new regime. Chapter 2 covers each one in depth. For now, know the menu and the limits.

children.text: Two Salaried Taxpayers, Two Different Winners

Suresh, 35, works at a Chennai auto-component company on ₹18 lakh. He maxes out 80C through EPF and PPF, puts ₹50,000 in NPS, pays ₹75,000 of health insurance for his family and his senior-citizen parents, and claims ₹2,40,000 of HRA. That is ₹5,67,500 of deductions including the standard deduction and professional tax. Ananya, 31, is a consultant in Mumbai on ₹25 lakh. She has the same 80C, NPS and health insurance, but pays ₹60,000 a month in rent in Bandra, giving her an HRA exemption of ₹5,95,000.

body.caption: Old vs New for Suresh and Ananya, Tax Year 2026-27

body.title: Show me the math for both

children.text: Ananya's HRA: basic salary ₹12,50,000, HRA received ₹6,25,000, rent paid ₹7,20,000 a year. The exemption is the least of HRA received (₹6,25,000), rent minus 10% of basic (₹7,20,000 minus ₹1,25,000, which is ₹5,95,000), and 50% of basic for a metro (₹6,25,000). So ₹5,95,000.

Ananya, old regime: deductions are ₹50,000 standard, ₹2,500 professional tax, ₹5,95,000 HRA, ₹1,50,000 80C, ₹50,000 NPS and ₹75,000 80D, total ₹9,22,500. Taxable income ₹15,77,500. Tax is ₹1,12,500 plus 30% of ₹5,77,500 (₹1,73,250), total ₹2,85,750. Cess ₹11,430. Tax: ₹2,97,180.

body.text: The old regime wins only when your deductions are large, genuine and already part of your life. Most often that means a big metro rent or a home loan stacked on top of 80C, NPS and health insurance.

body.title: Should Rakesh Buy a Policy to Save Tax?
body.scenario: Rakesh, 40, works at a Pune pharma company on ₹16 lakh. He lives in his parents' house, so he pays no rent and has no home loan. His EPF contribution and a term plan give him ₹1,20,000 under 80C. His neighbour, an insurance agent, urges him to switch to the old regime and buy a ₹30,000 a year endowment policy to fill up 80C and 'save tax'.
body.prompt: Compare Rakesh's tax in both regimes assuming he buys the policy. Is the agent's advice sound?
body.modelAnswer: No. With the policy, his old regime deductions are ₹50,000 standard, ₹2,500 professional tax and ₹1,50,000 under 80C, total ₹2,02,500. Taxable income is ₹13,97,500. Old regime tax is ₹1,12,500 plus 30% of ₹3,97,500 (₹1,19,250), total ₹2,31,750, plus ₹9,270 cess, which is ₹2,41,020. In the new regime taxable income is ₹15,25,000. Tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹3,25,000 (₹48,750), total ₹1,08,750, plus ₹4,350 cess, which is ₹1,13,100. The new regime is cheaper by ₹1,27,920 even after the extra deduction. Buying a ₹30,000 policy to chase a deduction he cannot benefit from would lock him into a low-return product for nothing.

body.title: Remember the Old Regime Limit
body.textWithBlank: In the old regime, the rebate makes tax nil only if taxable income is up to ₹___ lakh.
body.explanation: The old regime rebate is worth up to ₹12,500 and applies only up to ₹5 lakh of taxable income, with no marginal relief above it. Compare that with ₹12 lakh in the new regime.

body.title: List Your Genuine Old Regime Benefits
steps: Write down your annual rent paid and the HRA component on your payslip
Check your EPF contribution on the EPFO passbook, since it already counts towards 80C
Add PPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums and children's tuition fees you already pay
Note health insurance premiums for yourself, your family and your parents
Download your home loan interest certificate from your bank's net banking
Total everything and keep the number handy for the comparison in Chapter 3

points: The old regime is opt-in. You must actively choose it with your employer and in your return.
Its slabs jump from 5% to 20% at ₹5 lakh and reach 30% at just ₹10 lakh, but seniors get higher tax-free limits.
The old regime rebate is only up to ₹12,500, up to ₹5 lakh of taxable income, with no marginal relief.
On the same taxable income, the old regime always costs more. Deductions must close that gap for it to win.
The big benefits are HRA, 80C, NPS, 80D and home loan interest, most of which vanish in the new regime.
Never buy a financial product just for a deduction until you have checked that the old regime actually wins for you.
